title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 23
topics: A piece of art or performance that impressed you

questions: Do you enjoy drawing or painting, even just doodling while you're on the phone?
When was the last time you made something artistic, however small?
Were you encouraged to do art when you were at school, or was it treated as a minor subject?
Is there a kind of art you don't really get — something other people love but leaves you cold?
If you had a free afternoon and all the materials you wanted, what would you try to make?
How often do you visit museums or galleries — is it something you actually do, or something you mean to do?
Do you prefer wandering around on your own, or going with someone you can talk to about what you're seeing?
Do you remember a museum visit from your childhood? What stayed with you?
Do you think galleries in your country feel welcoming to ordinary people, or a bit intimidating?
In twenty years, do you think people will still visit museums in person, or will screens have taken over?

part2.title: Describe a piece of art or a performance that impressed you.
bullets: what it was and where you saw it
what it looked or sounded like
how you came to see it
part2.explain: and explain why it impressed you so much, and whether it changed how you think about art.
followups: Have you recommended it to anyone since?
Would you go back and see it again if you could?
Do you own anything connected to it — a print, a recording, a ticket you kept?

part3.q: Why do you think governments spend public money on art when there are hospitals and schools to fund?
followups: Is that spending easier to defend in rich countries than in poorer ones?
What would actually be lost if that funding stopped?

part3.q: In schools, art often loses timetable hours to subjects like maths and science. Is that the right priority?
followups: What do children get from art lessons that other subjects can't give them?
Who should make that decision — parents, teachers, or the government?

part3.q: Some people say a city without street art, music and theatre isn't really a city at all. Is that an exaggeration?
followups: Can you think of a place that proves your point?
Does this matter more to some generations than others?

part3.q: Do you think art made with artificial intelligence deserves to be called art?
followups: Does it matter whether a human or a machine made something, if the result moves people?
How might working artists feel about this?

part3.q: Who should decide what counts as good art — critics, the public, or the market?
followups: What happens when those three disagree?
Has the internet changed who gets to make that judgement?

part3.q: Some museums are free to enter while others charge quite a lot. Which approach is better for society?
followups: Does charging change who walks through the door?
How else could museums pay their bills?

part3.q: Wealthy people sometimes buy paintings purely as investments and store them in vaults. Is there anything wrong with that?
followups: Does the artist gain or lose anything when this happens?
Should there be limits on treating art as a financial asset?

part3.q: Why do some works of art stay famous for centuries while most are forgotten within a generation?
followups: Is lasting fame a reliable sign of quality?
Could something created today still matter in five hundred years?

part3.q: Is art that shocks or offends people doing something valuable, or just seeking attention?
followups: Where would you draw the line, if anywhere?
Has your view on this changed over time?

part3.q: Looking ahead, do you think human creativity will become more valued or less valued as machines learn to imitate it?
followups: What might people start paying for that they currently take for granted?
Is there any part of art you think machines will never reach?

fc: Sustains the Part 2 description of one artwork or performance without running dry — moving from what it was, to what it looked or sounded like, to why it landed.
Uses natural connectors for describing an experience ("the strange thing was", "what really got me", "even now") rather than listing features mechanically.
Handles the shift from describing a painting to debating public funding in Part 3 without the pace collapsing.
Extends abstract answers unprompted — the examiner shouldn't have to ask "why?" after every response about museums or funding.
Buys thinking time in English ("that's a genuinely hard one, because…") instead of long silences before questions like who decides what counts as art.
lr: Precise topic vocabulary: exhibition, sculpture, composition, striking, moving, breathtaking, curator, masterpiece, heritage.
Real collocations — "it took my breath away", "a permanent collection", "public funding for the arts" — not invented pairings.
Distinguishes near-synonyms accurately: impressive vs moving vs beautiful; a performance vs a show vs an exhibition.
Can talk about reactions to art with range: it stayed with me, it grew on me, I couldn't look away, it left me cold.
Moves into Part 3 register smoothly — subsidise, accessibility, cultural identity, commercialisation — without sounding like a memorised essay.
gra: Past narrative under control in Part 2: "I'd never seen anything like it", "we had been queuing for an hour when…".
Descriptive relative clauses that add detail without derailing: "the dancer, who must have been in her sixties, moved like…".
Conditionals for the funding and free-entry debates: "If museums charged nothing, they would have to…".
Concessive structures for balanced Part 3 answers: "Even though I see why hospitals come first, …".
Passives used naturally where the agent is unknown or unimportant: "it was painted over", "the piece is being restored".
pron: Clearly intelligible throughout — accent is fine; swallowed endings on words like "sculpture" and "exhibition" are not.
Stress lands on the evaluative words the topic invites: "it was genuinely unforgettable", not flat delivery.
Intonation lifts during the description of the artwork — a monotone account of something that supposedly impressed you undermines the content.
Multi-syllable topic words stressed correctly: exHIbition, phoTOgraphy, conTEMporary, inVESTment.
Chunks connected speech naturally ("piece_of_art", "work_of_art") rather than word-by-word delivery.

band9.part1: Answer in two to four sentences: direct answer first, then a reason or a tiny concrete detail. For "Is there a kind of art you don't really get?" a Band 9 answer commits and illustrates: "Honestly, video installations — I once stood in a dark room in front of a looping film of the sea for ten minutes waiting for something to happen, and everyone around me seemed transfixed. I'd rather look at one good drawing." That's specific, honest, and it answers the actual question instead of playing safe.
part2: Opening / context — name the piece or performance and where you saw it in one or two sentences, so the listener can picture the setting immediately.
The creator — say who made or performed it and how much you knew about them beforehand; "I'd never heard of her" is just as usable as naming someone famous.
Sensory description — spend real time on what it actually looked or sounded like; two or three concrete details (scale, colour, a single repeated note) beat ten vague adjectives.
How you came to see it — the accident or plan that put you in front of it; a chance encounter often makes the better story.
The moment of impact — pinpoint when it stopped being just something to look at; describe your physical reaction if there was one ("I realised I'd been holding my breath").
Reflection — close by answering the cue card's final question directly: what it changed about how you see art, even if the honest answer is "not everything, but this one thing".

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Why do you think governments spend public money on art when there are hospitals and schools to fund?
framework: Answer: take a position — e.g. because a society that only funds survival stops being somewhere people want to live.
Explain: give the mechanism — art builds shared identity and draws tourism and investment, so the spending partly pays for itself, and the sums involved are tiny next to health budgets.
Example: one concrete case — cities that invested in a landmark gallery or concert hall and saw the surrounding area revive, the way Bilbao did after the Guggenheim opened.

Alternative view: concede genuinely — when a health system is visibly failing, asking taxpayers to fund an opera house is a hard sell, and the people who benefit from subsidised art are often the better-off.

Evaluate: land the judgement — the real question isn't whether to fund art but which art, and funding that widens access earns its place more easily than funding that subsidises the already-comfortable.

mistakes.title: Describing the venue instead of the art
mistakes.detail: Candidates spend two minutes on the museum building, the ticket queue and the café, and thirty seconds on the actual painting or performance. The cue card is about the work itself — the setting is one sentence of context, not the story.

mistakes.title: Vague adjectives doing all the work
mistakes.detail: "It was amazing, really beautiful, so impressive" tells the examiner nothing and shows no lexical range. One concrete detail — the size of the canvas, the silence before the final note — is worth five empty superlatives.

mistakes.title: Claiming a famous work you can't describe
mistakes.detail: Choosing the Mona Lisa because it feels safe backfires when you can't say anything about it beyond "her smile is mysterious". A local street mural you actually stood in front of gives you far more to say.

mistakes.title: Skipping why it impressed you
mistakes.detail: The explain line carries the marks. A perfect description that never gets to the personal impact leaves the card half-answered — the examiner needs the "because", not just the "what".

mistakes.title: One-word Part 1 answers about drawing
mistakes.detail: "Do you enjoy drawing?" answered with "No, I'm bad at it" is a dead end. Even a negative answer extends naturally: what you do instead, when you stopped, whether you'd like to pick it up again.

mistakes.title: Turning the AI-art question into a technology lecture
mistakes.detail: The question is about what counts as art and what we value in human creativity — not how image generators work. Jargon about models and datasets earns nothing; a view about creativity does.

mistakes.title: Sitting on the fence about funding
mistakes.detail: "Art is important but hospitals are also important" with no follow-through is a Band 6 pattern. Commit — "I'd fund it, and here's the condition I'd attach" — and then concede the other side properly.

mistakes.title: Only talking about your own country's museums
mistakes.detail: Part 3 asks about societies in general. Anchoring every answer in one city you know is fine as illustration, but generalise beyond it — "in most big cities", "wherever entry is free" — or the answers stay Part 1-sized.

mistakes.title: Repeating 'art' in every sentence
mistakes.detail: The topic invites it. Vary the reference: the piece, the work, the exhibition, that performance, creative work, the arts. Lexical Resource is scored on exactly this kind of flexibility.

mistakes.title: Memorised 'importance of art' speech
mistakes.detail: Examiners hear the same rehearsed paragraph about art expressing emotions and reflecting culture several times a day. The questions here are sharper — funding trade-offs, AI, art as investment — and a stock speech simply doesn't answer them.
